item.title: Changes in large-scale circulation reshapes atmospheric river activity in northern Europe
item.description:
Post

There are conferences you look back on, conferences you are glad are over, and conferences you wish would never end. The 6th International Atmospheric Rivers Conference (IARC2026) was definitely the last kind.

I had the opportunity to present some of my research on how large-scale circulation shapes atmospheric river activity in Northern Europe. The conversations I had afterward with the community fostered plenty of new ideas.

But beyond the science, what made the conference truly special was the sense of community. As my PhD journey slowly comes to an end, this was my last conference as a PhD student.

Thank you to everyone! You made me feel so welcome!

I couldn’t have asked for a better way to mark the moment.

item.title: PS156: Geophysics Arctic Ocean Expedition on RV Polarstern
item.description:
Vessel Research Vessel Polarstern
Expedition PS156
Dates 6 August – 14 October 2026
Days at sea 70
Route Tromsø – Greenland – Lomonosov Ridge – Bremerhaven
Institutions Alfred Wegener Institute, University of Bergen and Tromsø, NORCE, MARUM, OGS

Post

Here I am, once again in the Arctic. This time aboard the legendary Polarstern, as part of the Lomonosov-Alpha-Morris Jesup Rise Expedition 1 (LAMEX 1), led by .

We left Tromsø on August 6 and our return to Bremerhaven is scheduled on October 14; yeah, exactly 70 days at sea. The expedition also serves as a scientific platform for the project. Check out the detailed scientific plan .

I am part of the Geophysics group, working with the Seismic team. Seismic surveys have added another layer of fascination/mystery to these expeditions as they allow us to look beneath the Arctic seafloor and “see” the geometry of sediment layers, in some places reaching up to about 2 km below the seabed. These sediments may contain a record of the Arctic Ocean reaching back roughly 20 million years, and potentially even further. Trying to grasp these timescales is, quite honestly, difficult.

Even more mysterious is that some sediment layers dating back 20 to 40 million years are unusually thin in some areas. Here, we are a bit like detectives, looking for where these layers are thicker and using these differences to understand why the same layers became much thinner in other parts of the Arctic Ocean.

This post comes with a small collection of moments from the expedition: deploying seismic instruments; preparing to fly by helicopter onto an ice floe near the Lomonosov Ridge to help with the deployment of an eXpendable Conductivity, Temperature and Depth (XCTD), using, surprisingly, a modified fishing rod; and, of course, spending time on a giant ice floe at the North Pole (that one could not be missed!). And then there is Polarstern, navigating through the ice in what sometimes feels like a lunar landscape. Listing these experiences in a few sentences does not really do them justice. Each one could probably need a chapter of its own.

It is a privilege to be here (for the second time; read about the first time and to contribute, even in a small way, to understanding one of the most remote and fascinating environments on Earth.

A round of thanks to everyone who makes this possible: Alfred Wegener Institute, Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research for providing the infrastructure and means for polar research; i2B Into The Blue for its scientific partnership; the Polarstern crew (Reederei F. Laeisz) for safely carrying us through the Arctic Ocean and supporting the deployment of our instruments; Deutscher Wetterdienst for providing dedicated weather forecasts through a meteorologist on board; Northern Helicopter GmbH for the pilots and engineers who make our helicopter operations possible and safe; And, last but certainly not least, thanks to for having me on board and for making me part of this adventure :)

Photo credits: black and white photos taken by Mario Hoppman, colored photo in front of the helicopter taken by Estella Weigelt

KH7010: i2B Arctic Ocean Expedition on RV Kronprins Haakon
item.description:
Vessel Research Vessel Kronprins Haakon
Expedition KH7010 (i2B)
Dates 16 August – 19 September 2025
Days at sea 35
Route Longyearbyen – Lomonosov Ridge / North Pole
Institutions University of Tromsø, NORCE, Alfred Wegener Institute, University of Bergen

Post

Standing on the sea ice, with over 4000 meters of ocean beneath my feet, felt almost unreal. I even played a soccer match there. Running in a survival suit was exhausting, but unforgettable.

This expedition is something I am still processing. It taught me a lot, not only in science but also about myself. I often think back to my little town in Veneto, where this journey began. From that starting point, with all my ambitions, doubts, fears, and failures, I step by step arrived here: at the North Pole, on a research vessel.

The path has not been easy. I have struggled many times, but I never gave up. And I could not have made it without the support of my family, friends, and even people who crossed my path only briefly.

Reaching the North Pole is something I will remember forever, especially in moments of struggle as a reminder of where I come from and how far my persistence and the support I have received can take me.

And yes, as if to make the moment even more surreal, a polar bear showed up later that day while we were sailing to the next station.

PS: A special thank you to Team B for making every shift fun and full of laughter.

PS145/1: Training Course on RV Polarstern
item.description:
Vessel Research Vessel Polarstern
Expedition PS145/1
Dates 24 November – 5 December 2024
Days at sea 12
Route Bremerhaven – Canary Islands
Institution Alfred Wegener Institute, Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research

Posts

I have just returned from one of my dream experiences: being at sea on a research vessel! I traveled from Bremerhaven to the Canary Islands aboard the icebreaker Polarstern during expedition PS145/1, where I participated in the Echosounding Training Cruise organized by POLMAR.

The program included lectures on the geophysical principles of echosounding, hands-on training in data acquisition, storage, and visualization using QGIS. Here there are some pictures of me engaged in these fascinating activities, including me deploying the Rosette with the CTD using the Laufkatze.

It was an incredible seagoing experience, and I am deeply grateful to AWI and POLMAR for making this possible!

Post

Outstanding experience in North Sea and Helgoland on the Research Vessel Heincke in April 2024.

I had the chance to join the physical oceanography group. I ran and processed Conductivity, Temperature, and Depth (CTD), Sound Velocity Profiler (SVP), and Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler (ADCP) measurements.
